subChunks.title: Relationships, Attraction & Group Processes
subChunks.hookHtml:
In 1898, Norman Triplett conducted what is sometimes credited as the first social-psychological experiment: he observed that competitive cyclists rode faster when racing against another cyclist than when racing against the clock alone. From that modest observation — that the mere presence of others can change individual performance — has grown a vast literature on how relationships form, how they sustain themselves, how they break down, and how groups think and decide collectively.

Relationships and group processes are not separate domains; they are the social architecture of human life. From the first spark of attraction to the deliberations of a hostile board meeting, from the warmth of a long marriage to the catastrophic decision-making of a war cabinet, the same psychological mechanisms — comparison, reward, identity, conformity, polarisation — operate at every level. Understanding them is understanding the structure of social life itself.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Theories of Interpersonal Attraction

Walster, Aronson, Abrahams & Rottman (1966) tested the matching hypothesis: people pair with partners of similar physical attractiveness. Their classic 'computer dance' study at the University of Minnesota randomly paired freshmen and found, surprisingly, that physical attractiveness was the strongest predictor of liking and desire to meet again — and that participants did not select for matched attractiveness in this initial encounter. Subsequent studies of established couples (e.g., Murstein, 1972) found stronger matching effects, suggesting that matching emerges through the selection process rather than as an initial preference. Modern dating-app data (Bruch & Newman, 2018) confirms that people pursue partners more attractive than themselves but tend to form relationships with similarly attractive partners.

Donn Byrne's (1971) similarity-attraction hypothesis proposed that we are attracted to people who hold similar attitudes, derived from the rewarding nature of attitudinal validation. Byrne's bogus stranger paradigm presented participants with attitude profiles supposedly belonging to a stranger and varied the proportion of shared attitudes. Liking increased linearly with attitude similarity, a finding replicated extensively. The proximity effect (Festinger, Schachter & Back, 1950, in their MIT housing study) demonstrated that physical and functional distance powerfully shape friendship formation — residents who lived closer to one another, especially on the same floor, were significantly more likely to become friends.

Robert Zajonc's (1968) mere exposure effect demonstrated that repeated exposure to a stimulus, in the absence of reinforcement, increases liking — even when participants cannot recall having seen the stimulus before. The effect operates for nonsense words, Chinese ideographs, photographs of faces, and abstract figures, and explains why proximity produces friendship (proximity increases exposure, which increases liking). Meta-analyses (Bornstein, 1989) confirm the effect with moderate effect sizes, with optimal exposure frequency typically below ten repetitions and effects sometimes reversing with overexposure.

Filter Theory and the Development of Relationships

Kerckhoff & Davis (1962) proposed filter theory: prospective partners pass through a series of filters as a relationship develops. Initial filters include sociological variables (proximity, ethnicity, social class) — limiting the field of potential partners. Subsequent filters include attitudinal similarity — important early in relationships. Later filters include complementarity of needs — important in established relationships. The model has received mixed empirical support, with subsequent research suggesting the temporal sequence is not as orderly as originally proposed.

Social Exchange, Equity and Investment

Thibaut & Kelley's (1959) social exchange theory applies economic reasoning to relationships: people evaluate relationships by their rewards minus costs, comparing the outcome to (a) their comparison level (the outcome they feel they deserve, based on past experience) and (b) their comparison level for alternatives (the best outcome available elsewhere). Satisfaction depends on the first comparison; commitment depends on the second.

Walster, Walster & Berscheid's (1978) equity theory modifies social exchange by arguing that perceived fairness — not absolute rewards — predicts satisfaction. Both under-benefit (feeling exploited) and over-benefit (feeling guilty) produce dissatisfaction. The theory has been criticised on the grounds that close relationships may operate by communal rather than exchange norms (Clark & Mills, 1979) — in communal relationships, partners respond to one another's needs without expectation of reciprocation, and explicit accounting of give-and-take is felt to undermine the relationship.

Caryl Rusbult's (1980) investment model extended social exchange by adding a third determinant of commitment: investment size — resources (time, emotion, shared possessions) that would be lost if the relationship ended. Commitment is thus a function of satisfaction, perceived alternatives, and investment. The model has been extensively tested and predicts relationship persistence even in abusive or unsatisfying relationships, where high investment and low perceived alternatives sustain commitment despite low satisfaction (Rusbult & Martz, 1995).

Maintenance and Breakdown of Relationships

Steve Duck's (1982) four-phase model of relationship dissolution proposes: (1) intra-psychic phase — private brooding on dissatisfaction; (2) dyadic phase — open confrontation between partners; (3) social phase — engagement of social network in the dissolution; and (4) grave-dressing phase — public narrative-construction about why the relationship ended. Duck later added a fifth resurrection phase in which lessons are extracted for future relationships. The model is largely descriptive and has been criticised for cultural specificity (it best describes Western individualist dissolution patterns) and for not specifying when phases occur or how long they last.

Adult Attachment Theory

Cindy Hazan & Phillip Shaver (1987) applied Bowlby's infant attachment theory to adult romantic relationships, proposing that internal working models formed in childhood shape adult romantic attachment. They identified three styles paralleling Ainsworth's infant categories: secure (comfortable with intimacy and autonomy), anxious-ambivalent (craving closeness, fearing abandonment), and avoidant (uncomfortable with closeness, preferring emotional distance). Their newspaper survey of self-classified attachment styles found these styles predicted distinctive patterns of romantic experience consistent with theory.

Subsequent work, particularly Bartholomew & Horowitz (1991), refined the model into a two-dimensional structure (anxiety and avoidance) with four resulting prototypes. Mikulincer & Shaver's (2007) comprehensive review documents that attachment style predicts relationship satisfaction, response to conflict, sexual behaviour, and even physiological stress responses. However, the assumption of strong continuity from infant to adult attachment has been disputed: Fraley (2002) found longitudinal continuity coefficients of approximately 0.40, indicating substantial but far from perfect stability.

Parasocial Relationships and Online Dating

Horton & Wohl (1956) introduced the term parasocial relationship to describe one-sided emotional bonds formed by audiences with media figures. Decades of research demonstrate that these relationships activate many of the same psychological mechanisms as reciprocal relationships, and may provide genuine emotional benefits for individuals with limited social opportunities — though they can also displace reciprocal relationships in extreme cases.

Finkel et al.'s (2012) influential review of online dating distinguished three core promises of dating sites: access to potential partners (genuinely expanded), matching via algorithms (no convincing evidence that algorithms outperform random matching), and communication before meeting (mixed effects on relationship outcomes). The review argued that the algorithmic matching claims of major dating sites lacked empirical support — partner compatibility cannot be reliably predicted from self-report profile data prior to interaction. More recent work (Joel, Eastwick & Finkel, 2017) using machine learning on extensive pre-meeting data confirms that initial attraction is largely unpredictable from pre-meeting characteristics.

Group Processes: Groupthink

Irving Janis (1972, 1982) coined groupthink following case analyses of foreign policy disasters including the Bay of Pigs invasion. Groupthink occurs when cohesive in-groups, under stress and isolated from dissent, prioritise consensus over critical evaluation. Symptoms include illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, stereotyping of out-groups, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, direct pressure on dissenters, and self-appointed mindguards. Janis's case-based methodology has been criticised — selective case selection, retrospective bias, and lack of experimental control — and subsequent experimental tests have produced mixed results. However, the concept has remained heuristically valuable for analysing organisational decision failures.

Social Loafing and Social Facilitation

Maximilian Ringelmann's late-19th-century rope-pulling studies (rediscovered by Ingham et al., 1974) found that individual effort decreased as group size increased — even when individuals believed they were pulling alone. Latané, Williams & Harkins (1979) replicated and named this social loafing, attributing it to diffusion of responsibility, evaluation apprehension reduction, and matching of perceived equity. Meta-analysis (Karau & Williams, 1993) confirms the effect with moderate effect sizes and identifies moderators: loafing is reduced when contributions are identifiable, when the task is meaningful, and when group cohesion is high.

In direct tension with loafing is Triplett's (1898) original social facilitation finding: the presence of others enhances performance, at least on simple tasks. Zajonc (1965) reconciled the apparent contradiction with his drive theory: the presence of others increases arousal, which enhances dominant responses — facilitating simple/well-learned tasks and impairing complex/novel tasks. The model has been supported by extensive research across human and animal subjects.

Deindividuation

Philip Zimbardo (1969), drawing on Le Bon's earlier crowd psychology, proposed that deindividuating conditions — anonymity, group immersion, reduced self-awareness — release antisocial behaviour normally inhibited by accountability and self-monitoring. His classic study found that hooded participants (anonymity condition) delivered longer shocks to a victim than identifiable participants. The Stanford Prison Experiment (Haney, Banks & Zimbardo, 1973) is frequently cited as further evidence, though it has been heavily criticised on methodological and ethical grounds (Le Texier, 2019, demonstrates that participants were extensively coached and that the 'spontaneous' brutalisation was substantially scripted).

Reicher, Spears & Postmes's (1995) SIDE model (Social Identity Model of Deindividuation Effects) provides a contemporary alternative: anonymity does not release suppressed antisocial impulses but rather shifts identity from personal to social — making salient group identity behaviours follow. Under this model, deindividuation can produce prosocial behaviour just as readily as antisocial behaviour, depending on which group identity is salient. The SIDE model has empirical support and offers a more theoretically sophisticated account than classical deindividuation theory.

Group Polarisation

Stoner's (1961) finding that group discussion produces decisions more extreme than the average pre-discussion individual position has been replicated extensively under the broader rubric of group polarisation. Discussion does not moderate group positions toward the centre; rather, groups become more extreme in the direction of their pre-discussion lean. Two mechanisms are typically invoked: persuasive arguments theory (group members hear additional arguments supporting the dominant position) and social comparison (members shift positions to differentiate themselves favourably from others). The effect has obvious implications for jury deliberation, social media echo chambers, and political radicalisation. Bail et al. (2018) provide recent evidence relevant to contemporary applications: exposure to opposing political views on Twitter actually increased polarisation rather than reducing it, suggesting that simple cross-cutting exposure is not a sufficient remedy.

Minority Influence Revisited

Returning to Moscovici (1969, 1980), the relationship between group processes and minority influence highlights an important caveat to groupthink and polarisation: the presence of consistent dissent can disrupt these processes, promote divergent thinking, and produce better-quality decisions. Janis himself recommended structural antidotes including the appointment of devil's advocates — an institutionalised minority influence designed to break groupthink before it produces catastrophic decisions.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen begins with Festinger, Schachter and Back's MIT housing study from 1950 — a friendship-network diagram of an apartment block, with thick lines connecting neighbouring residents.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Most of your future friends are within fifty feet of where you sit. Festinger's data showed that the probability of friendship dropped sharply with distance — and not just physical distance. Functional distance mattered too: people who passed each other on a stairwell had a stronger friendship probability than those who lived on different floors. Proximity, plus mere exposure, plus repeated low-stakes interaction. That's most of how friendships start.
She introduces Rusbult's investment model and shows a graph: high investment, low alternatives — relationship persists even when satisfaction is low.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Rusbult's contribution was profound for understanding why people stay in relationships that look, from the outside, unsustainable. Satisfaction is one factor. Alternatives are another. Investment — what you would lose — is the third. This is why people stay in unhappy marriages, unsatisfying jobs, unfulfilling friendships. The economic logic is sound, even when the outcome is sad.
She projects Janis's groupthink symptoms beside the Bay of Pigs case timeline.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Janis identified eight symptoms of groupthink, but the underlying mechanism is simple: a cohesive group, under pressure, isolated from dissent, will reach a consensus that no individual member would have endorsed alone. Kennedy's advisors privately had grave doubts about the Bay of Pigs invasion. None voiced them. The structural remedies — devil's advocates, outside consultants, anonymous polling — are all attempts to import minority influence into a group designed to suppress it.
She turns to Bail et al.'s 2018 Twitter study — exposure to opposing political views increased rather than decreased polarisation.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: This finding is humbling for anyone who believed simply 'getting out of the echo chamber' would heal polarisation. Bail and colleagues paid Twitter users to follow accounts from the opposing political side. After a month, Republicans were more conservative, and Democrats were slightly more liberal. The contact hypothesis assumes contact under specific conditions. Hostile Twitter exchanges meet none of them.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided Practice — Applying the Investment Model

Scenario: A clinical psychologist is working with a client who has remained in a relationship marked by frequent conflict and low satisfaction for over ten years. The client describes their partner as 'family' and feels unable to leave despite acknowledging the relationship's costs. They report having no other romantic prospects in mind and having built a home, social life, and shared finances with their partner over the past decade.

Using Rusbult's (1980) investment model and Thibaut & Kelley's (1959) social exchange theory, analyse the psychological factors sustaining the client's commitment. In your answer, distinguish satisfaction, perceived alternatives, and investment, and explain how this framework can inform therapeutic conversations about relationship choices.

Guidance: Apply specific concepts from each model to the scenario. Aim for 110–130 words.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Thibaut and Kelley’s (1959) social exchange theory explains that while the client’s satisfaction is low—due to high relational costs (conflict) outweighing rewards—their commitment is sustained by their comparison level for alternatives. Perceiving "no other romantic prospects," the client lacks viable alternatives that exceed their current situation.

Rusbult’s (1980) investment model further clarifies this entrapment by introducing investment size as a critical determinant of commitment. Over ten years, the client has accumulated massive intrinsic and extrinsic investments: a shared home, combined finances, and intertwined social networks. Leaving would mean forfeiting these profound investments.

Therapeutically, this framework normalises the client's ambivalence. Conversations can shift from a simplistic "why don't you leave" approach to a structured exploration of how to mitigate the perceived loss of investments, or how to gradually build independent social and financial alternatives, thereby altering the commitment calculus.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Groupthink and Social Media Polarisation

A government enquiry is examining how a series of departmental decisions led to a significant policy failure. The enquiry hears that the relevant team was highly cohesive, worked under intense time pressure, and rarely consulted outside expertise. Separately, recent research has highlighted growing political polarisation on social media platforms despite — or because of — exposure to opposing viewpoints.

Drawing on Janis's (1972, 1982) groupthink theory, Stoner's (1961) group polarisation research, and Bail et al.'s (2018) Twitter exposure study, critically analyse both phenomena. In your answer, identify the structural and psychological mechanisms driving poor collective decision-making in each context, and propose evidence-based interventions to mitigate each problem.

Write at least 140 words in paragraphs. Include named studies, theoretical mechanisms, and concrete recommendations.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Janis's (1972, 1982) groupthink theory identifies the conditions under which cohesive groups produce defective decisions: high cohesion, structural insulation from dissent, time pressure, and directive leadership. Symptoms include illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, self-censorship, and direct pressure on dissenters. The departmental team described in the enquiry exhibits the classic risk profile — cohesion, time pressure, and limited external consultation — all factors that predict the suppression of doubt and the production of decisions no individual member would have endorsed alone. The structural antidotes Janis himself proposed include the formal appointment of devil's advocates, the use of outside consultants at key decision points, anonymous polling of group members, and the explicit division of the team into subgroups tasked with critiquing one another's recommendations.

Stoner's (1961) group polarisation research demonstrates that groups do not converge toward the centre during discussion but instead shift more extremely in the direction of their pre-discussion lean. Two mechanisms — persuasive arguments theory and social comparison — explain the effect. In contemporary digital contexts, Bail et al.'s (2018) Twitter exposure study significantly complicates the assumption that exposure to opposing views reduces polarisation. Their experiment paid Twitter users to follow accounts from the opposing political side; after one month, Republicans became more conservative and Democrats slightly more liberal, suggesting that hostile cross-cutting exposure can intensify rather than moderate group attitudes.

The two findings converge on a common implication: high-quality collective decision-making requires more than the mere presence of dissent or exposure. It requires structural conditions — Allport's (1954) contact-hypothesis conditions translated to deliberative contexts — including equal status, common goals, and institutional support. Practical interventions include red-team processes, structured deliberation formats designed to surface minority views, deliberative polling, and platform-level design changes that reduce the emotional intensity of cross-cutting exposure while preserving its informational value.
